Tariff. A tax imposed on imported goods when they cross a nation's border. Tariffs raise the price of foreign goods, making domestic producers more competitive. While tariffs protect domestic jobs and industries in the short run, they also reduce consumer choice, raise prices for consumers, and invite retaliation from trading partners. Tariffs are a tool of protectionism—the deliberate restriction of imports to shield domestic industries.

Tariffs take two main forms. An ad valorem tariff is a percentage tax on the import price, like twenty-five percent. A specific tariff is a fixed dollar amount per unit, like two dollars per barrel of oil. Both raise the price of imported goods, shifting demand toward domestic substitutes and allowing domestic producers to expand output.

Who wins and loses? Domestic producers in protected industries win. Workers in those industries benefit in the short run. Domestic consumers lose because they pay higher prices. Foreign exporters lose because they sell less. Other domestic industries that rely on cheap imports as inputs lose. The net effect is typically deadweight loss. The gains to producers don't fully offset losses to consumers and the forgone benefits of trade.

Historically, tariffs have played different roles. In the mercantilist era, they maintained trade surpluses and accumulated precious metals. The Smoot-Hawley Tariff of nineteen thirty raised U.S. tariffs to protect against the Great Depression. Trading partners retaliated, worsening the crisis. Post-World War II, the General Agreement on Tariffs and Trade and the World Trade Organization gradually lowered tariffs, though many sectors remain protected.

Tariffs serve strategic purposes. Infant industry protection shields new industries in developing countries until they gain competitiveness. National security tariffs protect production of critical goods like semiconductors and military equipment. Tariff threats serve as negotiating leverage in trade talks.

Tariffs embody a perennial political tension. Free trade increases overall economic efficiency and consumer welfare, but the benefits are diffuse. The costs are concentrated—a few industries lose jobs and market share. This asymmetry makes tariff protection politically durable despite its efficiency costs. The political appeal of protecting jobs competes with the economic reality that tariffs ultimately hurt more consumers than they help workers in protected industries. Tariff policy is a litmus test for understanding the gap between political economy and textbook economics.
